title: Sealing a Garage Floor: Hot-Tire Pickup, Salt and Oil
metaTitle: Sealing a Garage Floor: Salt, Oil & Tire Marks
metaDescription: Garage floors take a unique beating from winter salt, oil drips and hot tires. Here is how proper sealing protects concrete against all three in Ontario.
excerpt: A garage floor faces a different kind of abuse than a driveway or patio: tracked-in salt, oil drips, and hot tire pickup. Here is how sealing addresses each one.
heroAlt: Freshly sealed garage floor in Oxford County Ontario with an even matte finish resisting oil stains and tire marks
keyTakeaways: Garage floors face three distinct stresses that driveways and patios rarely see together: tracked-in road salt, oil and fluid drips, and hot tire pickup marks.
Hot tire pickup happens when warm tires soften an unsealed or poorly sealed coating and lift small pieces of it as the vehicle moves, and it is largely preventable with the right sealer.
Polyurethane and quality acrylic sealers both resist oil staining far better than bare concrete, which is porous enough to absorb drips within minutes.
Winter salt tracked in on tires and boots is one of the fastest ways an unsealed garage floor develops surface scaling and pitting.
A Matte finish is the most popular choice for garage floors because it hides everyday scuffs and tire marks better than a glossier sheen.

body.text: Of all the concrete surfaces around a Southwestern Ontario home, the garage floor probably takes the most varied abuse and gets the least attention. A driveway deals mainly with weather and traffic. A patio deals mainly with weather and foot traffic. A garage floor deals with all of that plus a rotating cast of specific stresses: hot tires rolling in straight off the highway, oil and transmission fluid dripping from parked vehicles, and a steady tracking-in of winter road salt every time someone pulls in during December through March. Sealing a garage floor properly means addressing all three, not just applying the same coating you would use outside and hoping for the best.

Hot-tire pickup is the small, often circular patches of coating that lift off a garage floor where a vehicle's tires sit, usually noticed as the tire tread pattern faintly embossed into the sealer or, in worse cases, as small chunks of coating stuck to the tire itself. It happens because tires coming off a highway drive, especially in summer, retain significant heat, and that heat can soften certain coatings enough that the tire's weight and slight movement while parking pulls a bit of the softened material away from the concrete. It is more common with lower-quality or improperly cured coatings, and less common with a properly applied sealer that has been given adequate time to cure before vehicles are parked on it.

The fix starts with product choice and application, not with a workaround after the fact. A sealer designed and applied for garage floor use, given full curing time before any vehicle traffic, resists this far better than a rushed job or an outdoor-grade product applied without the extra attention a garage floor needs. If you already have tire marks embedded in an old coating, that is generally a sign the existing sealer has failed and needs to be assessed for a recoat rather than a spot fix.
Oil, fluid drips, and everyday stains

Bare, unsealed concrete is porous, which means oil, transmission fluid, antifreeze, and other automotive fluids soak in within minutes rather than sitting on the surface where they can be wiped up. Once a stain has penetrated bare concrete, it is often permanent, or at best fades only slightly with aggressive cleaning. A properly sealed garage floor changes that equation. A quality sealer forms a barrier on and just below the surface that keeps oil and fluids from soaking in, giving you time to wipe up a drip before it becomes a stain. This is one of the most immediately noticeable benefits homeowners mention after sealing a garage floor: a spill that would have ruined bare concrete now just needs a rag.

This protection matters just as much for a workshop or hobby garage as it does for daily vehicle parking. Anyone doing basic maintenance, changing their own oil, or storing a lawn tractor or snowblower over winter benefits from a floor that shrugs off the inevitable small drips that come with that kind of use.
Salt: the winter problem most people overlook

Driveways get the credit for dealing with winter salt, but garage floors absorb just as much of it, if not more, because it gets tracked in on tires and boots and then sits and melts on the floor rather than draining away the way it does outside. That salty meltwater pools in low spots or along the edges of a garage floor and, on bare or poorly sealed concrete, drives the same freeze-thaw scaling and surface pitting you would see on an unprotected driveway, except indoors where it is less visible until the damage is significant. Salt residue left sitting on unsealed concrete also tends to leave a chalky white staining, sometimes called efflorescence, as it draws moisture and minerals to the surface. A sealed garage floor sheds that salty water instead of absorbing it, which is one of the more practical, if less discussed, reasons to seal a garage floor in a region that gets a real Ontario winter.
A garage floor that pools salty meltwater every winter is absorbing the same freeze-thaw stress as an unsealed driveway, just indoors and out of sight until cracking shows up.

items: Hot tire pickup: prevented by proper product choice and full cure time before vehicle traffic
Oil and fluid stains: blocked by a sealer barrier that keeps drips from soaking into porous concrete
Tracked-in road salt: shed off the surface instead of pooling and driving freeze-thaw scaling
Everyday scuffs and tire marks: minimized visually with a Matte finish rather than a high-gloss sheen

body.text: The sealing process for a garage floor

All-Seal follows the same core method on a garage floor as any other surface, with attention to the specific conditions a garage presents. The floor is thoroughly cleaned, which for a garage often means dealing with existing oil residue and ground-in dirt that a simple pressure wash alone might not fully lift. Any cracks or joints are repaired at this stage, since garage floors often have expansion joints or minor settling cracks that need attention before a sealer goes down evenly. The surface is given time to dry completely, which matters more indoors where airflow is limited compared to an open driveway. Once dry, the sealer is applied for even coverage, and enough cure time is allowed before the garage goes back into daily use, particularly before parking a vehicle back on it, to avoid the hot-tire pickup issue described above.
Choosing the right sheen for a garage

Matte is the most commonly recommended finish for garage floors, and for good reason. A garage floor sees more everyday wear in a smaller, more visible space than most outdoor surfaces, from tire marks to dropped tools to foot traffic in and out of a house entry door. A Matte finish has a more natural, less reflective look that tends to hide scuffs, dust, and minor surface marks better than a glossier sheen would, which keeps the floor looking clean between cleanings. That said, Semi-Gloss and High Gloss are also available for anyone who prefers a brighter look, and an anti-slip additive can be added to any sheen, which is worth considering near a garage entry that gets wet from snow and rain tracked in during winter. You can compare all three sheen options in more detail at /finishes.

Garage floor sealing tends to be one of the most requested services in areas with real winters and daily commuting, which describes most of the region All-Seal serves. Homeowners in Woodstock and Oxford County, along with St. Thomas, Brantford, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, and Cambridge, all deal with the same combination of highway salt exposure and cold-weather parking that makes garage floor sealing worthwhile. Detached garages that double as workshops, and attached garages that serve as the main household entry point through winter, both benefit, since both see the same repeated cycle of salt, moisture, and vehicle traffic all winter long.
When to seal, and how long it lasts

Garage floors generally fall on the shorter end of the sealer lifespan range, often needing a recoat every 2 to 3 years given the combination of salt exposure and vehicle traffic. Watch for the same water-bead test that applies to any sealed concrete: if water no longer beads up and instead soaks into the surface, or if oil starts leaving faint stains it did not used to leave, the sealer has worn thin enough to need attention. Full details on how sealer lifespan works across different surfaces are covered in our guide at /resources/how-long-does-concrete-sealer-last-in-ontario.

faq.q: What causes hot tire pickup on a sealed garage floor?
faq.a: Hot tire pickup happens when heat from a tire softens the sealer coating enough for the tire to lift small pieces as the vehicle is parked or moved, usually the result of an improperly cured or lower-quality coating rather than sealing itself.

faq.q: Can sealing really prevent oil stains on a garage floor?
faq.a: Yes. A sealed floor keeps oil and other fluids from soaking into the porous concrete, giving you time to wipe up a drip before it becomes a permanent stain, unlike bare concrete which absorbs spills within minutes.

faq.q: Does winter salt actually damage a garage floor?
faq.a: Yes. Salt tracked in on tires and boots pools and melts on the floor, and on unsealed concrete it can drive freeze-thaw scaling and leave chalky white staining, the same damage salt causes on an unprotected driveway.

faq.q: What finish is best for a garage floor?
faq.a: Matte is the most popular choice for garage floors because its natural, less reflective look hides everyday scuffs and tire marks better than a glossier sheen, though Semi-Gloss and High Gloss are also available.

faq.q: How often does a garage floor need resealing?
faq.a: Garage floors typically need resealing every 2 to 3 years given the combination of winter salt exposure and daily vehicle traffic, similar to a driveway.

faq.q: How soon can I park in the garage after sealing?
faq.a: The sealer needs full cure time before vehicles return, which your All-Seal technician will confirm based on conditions, since parking too soon is one of the main causes of hot-tire pickup.
